Over the decade, New York Watch Week has grown from a tiny affair into a massive calendar of events featuring everything from massive luxury brands to the most exciting players on the independent scene. Most important for our purposes is that the event has grown large enough to demand that brands not only show up to meet collectors at functions like WatchTime and WindUp Watch Fair, but also reward us with brand-new pieces.

There has been no shortage of great watches released this week by the likes of Ming, TAG Heuer, and Brew. To be fair, not all of the pieces below are technically NYWW releases, but this week has swelled enough that brands now stuff the calendar to take advantage of the extra eyeballs on the industry.

That makes Brew’s yellow cab-inspired piece an even more welcome addition to this roster of drops. The coffee-inspired brand updated its flagship Metric design with the colors of New York’s most beloved icons. The electric shade of yellow really works for me—I discovered I have a real thing for the color this year—and the checkerboard pattern makes it impossible to mistake what you’re looking at. With “New York” printed at 6 o’clock, the only detail this piece is missing is the ability to shout, “Ay, I’m walking here.” And if you’re asking what this has to do with a brand that takes its cues from the world of coffee, consider what you may need a lot of in the City That Never Sleeps. The new $495 Metric drops Monday, October 19th on Brew’s website. —Cam Wolf

Hermès H08 Bleu de Malte and Blanc Chantilly

blocks.x: Since its launch in 2021, the Hermès H08 has come to represent the luxury brand’s revitalized watch department. The sporty tonneau-shaped case is a departure from the brand’s dressier models such as the Arceau and Cape Cod, and even includes a monopusher chronograph within the lineup. Two cool new additions to the collection are debuting this week: while Bleu de Malte mixes a braided glass-fiber composite case, a satin-brushed blue ceramic bezel, and blue accents throughout a sandblasted dial, Blanc Chantilly features a white ceramic bezel and a white lacquered dial. This is one of those watches that's not technically a NYWW debut, but, in an effort to show you all the best stuff coming this week, we're including it. —OH
TAG Heuer Formula 1 Solargraph x Oracle Red Bull Racing

blocks.c: Image may contain Wristwatch Arm Body Part and Person

blocks.x: The rebirth of the Formula 1 collection has been a smash hit, bringing back a childhood favorite for millennials while introducing younger wearers to a colorful, more affordable side of the historic brand. A new version made for the Oracle Red Bull Racing team should keep the watch’s hot streak going. The new model features a blue bezel and matching dial with a red minute track and white luminous indices. Unlike many of the other F1s, it ships on a stainless steel bracelet that matches its tonneau-shaped case. The $2,250 price tag is a pretty great deal for a modern TAG Heuer. —OH
Chopard L.U.C. Full Strike Día de Los Muertos

blocks.c: Image may contain Wristwatch Arm Body Part and Person

blocks.x: By far the most metal watch in a week full of them, Chopard’s L.U.C. Full Strike Día de Los Muertos celebrates Mexico’s Day of the Dead in Swiss fashion, with a stylized calavera skull executed with eggshell and blue-straw marquetry in a process that takes some 160 hours. Housed in a 42.5mm 18K ethical rose gold case, the watch is powered by the maison’s L.U.C Calibre 08.01-L, the brand’s first in-house minute repeater, which chimes out the time like it's a tiny gorgeous song. Designed with monobloc construction, its sapphire and gongs are constructed from a single piece of sapphire, which creates a particularly pure and pleasing tone. Visible from the watch’s caseback, the movement has no less than five patents for its exceptionally complex functionality. —OH
Arnold & Son DSTB Stop-Seconds Red Gold Cliff Grey and Platinum Kingsand

blocks.c: Image may contain Wristwatch Arm Body Part and Person

blocks.x: Limited to 18 pieces each, the new Dial-Side True Beat Stop-Seconds in Red Gold Cliff Grey or Platinum Kingsand are tributes to the marine chronometer—a type of clock that allowed seafarers to calculate longitude during long voyages, thereby ensuring accurate navigation. A sophisticated in-house movement, the automatic cal. A&S6303, powers a “true beat” (or “dead beat”) seconds display that ticks along once per second like a quartz watch, thus allowing the wearer to determine the time as accurately as possible. Additionally, it features a stop-seconds (or “hacking”) feature, which allows it to be set to a precise time signal. —OH
